title: Family, age, and how to address people
goal: Talk about your family, ask someone's age without sounding nosy, and address people with the right term — in Laos, addressing people correctly matters more than perfect grammar.
bekal: family members and the older/younger order
ask someone's age with ອາຍຸຈັກປີ
address people with ອ້າຍ ເອື້ອຍ ນ້ອງ ລຸງ ປ້າ
married/not yet married with ແຕ່ງງານ

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — At Bounmy's house, Sunday afternoon
dialogs.intro: Budi is invited to eat at Bounmy's house and meets his family. Notice that everyone is addressed with a kinship term, almost never by name alone.

notes: **Lao kinship terms are divided by OLDER vs. YOUNGER, not just by gender.** *ອ້າຍ âai* is an older brother, *ເອື້ອຍ ʉ̂ʉay* an older sister, and *ນ້ອງ náwng* is a younger sibling — brother or sister. To be specific, add *ຊາຍ sáai* (male) or *ສາວ sǎao* (female): *ນ້ອງສາວ* (younger sister).

**Kinship terms are used for STRANGERS too.** Someone your older sibling's age is *ອ້າຍ* or *ເອື້ອຍ*; someone your parents' age is *ລຸງ lung* (uncle) or *ປ້າ pâa* (auntie); someone younger is *ນ້ອງ*. Calling a server at a food stall *ເອື້ອຍ* is far warmer and more polite than calling her nothing at all.

**ອາຍຸຈັກປີ aa-nyu ják pii = "how old are you," and it is NOT a nosy question in Laos.** Age decides which term people use, so it gets asked earlier than Westerners are used to. Answering it isn't considered personal either.

**ຂອງ khǎwng = "of, belonging to," and it goes BEFORE the owner.** *ແມ່ຂອງຂ້ອຍ* (my mother), *ລົດຂອງລາວ* (his car). In fast speech *ຂອງ* is often dropped: *ແມ່ຂ້ອຍ* is enough, and that's actually what you'll hear most.

**ຄິດຮອດ khit hâwt = "to miss," literally "thoughts reach."** It's a very Lao expression and used constantly — for family, friends, even places. *ຄິດຮອດເຈົ້າ* (I miss you) isn't romantic; it's ordinary and warm.
**ຍັງບໍ່ທັນແຕ່ງງານ nyáng bàw than tèng-ngáan = "not married yet."** Notice *ຍັງ…ບໍ່ທັນ*, meaning "not yet," not "not." Answering *ບໍ່ແຕ່ງງານ* means "I don't marry" — a completely different statement.

**ກິນເຂົ້າແລ້ວບໍ່ kin khào lèeo bàw = "have you eaten?" is a greeting, not a question.** It works much like "How's it going?" in English. The right answer: *ກິນແລ້ວ* (yes) or *ຍັງ* (not yet) — and if you say "not yet," be ready to actually be fed.
**ໝູ່ mùu = "friend."** *ໝູ່ຮ່ວມງານ* (coworker), *ໝູ່ດີ* (good friend). ⚠️ In Thai a similar word means "group"; in Lao it simply means friend, and it's one of the words you'll hear most.
**ນັ່ງກ່ອນ nàng kàwn = "sit down first."** *ກ່ອນ kàwn* after a verb means "first, ahead": *ໄປກ່ອນ* (go on ahead), *ກິນກ່ອນ* (eat first). It's also the most common way to say goodbye.

grammars.title: Family: from grandparents to grandchildren
after: ⚠️ *ແຟນ féen* means "boyfriend/girlfriend" **and** "spouse," for men and women alike. It isn't the English word "fan." Asking *ມີແຟນບໍ່* (do you have a partner?) is ordinary small talk in Laos, not flirting.

Call them
Say it

blocks.text: The practical rule: **when in doubt, go one step up.** Calling someone your own age *ອ້າຍ* feels respectful and pleasant; calling someone clearly older *ນ້ອງ* feels rude. Erring on the side of respect never costs you anything.

A note about monks: women **may not** touch a monk or hand anything directly to him — items are placed on a cloth the monk spreads out. This isn't about manners but monastic rules, and breaking it means the monk has to undergo a purification ritual.

sections.title: Personality: describing the people you talk about

blocks.text: The prefix **ຂີ້- *khîi-*** marks traits that lean negative or bad habits: *ຂີ້ຄ້ານ* (lazy), *ຂີ້ອາຍ* (shy), *ຂີ້ຮ້າຍ khîi-hâai* (ugly), *ຂີ້ຕົວະ khîi-tùa* (liar). If you hear *khîi-* at the start of a word, brace yourself: what follows isn't a compliment.

⚠️ Commenting on someone's weight is far more ordinary in Laos than in most Western countries — *ຕຸ້ຍຂຶ້ນເນາະ* (you've put on weight, huh) can be friendly small talk, not an insult. You don't have to copy the habit, but don't be shocked when you hear it.
